This evaluates mastery of branchless bit tricks and fast bit-scanning techniques essential in performance-critical code like network filtering.

- Branchless bit manipulation

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to implement a rotation primitive with wrap-around using only shifts and masks, including masking to handle large r and the n=0 edge case.

## Key Concepts
- Circular shift using (x << n) | (x >> (32 - n))
- Masking r with 31 to confine to 0..31
- Edge-case n=0 preserves x exactly

## Code Example
```c
static inline uint32_t rotl32(uint32_t x, unsigned r) {
  unsigned n = r & 31; // 0..31
  return (x << n) | (x >> (32 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to 64-bit rotates?
- What are the potential performance differences vs. compiler intrinsics like _rotl?
- How would you test across boundary values (r=0, r=31, r=32, r=33)?

## Why This Is Asked

Assess practical bit-manipulation intuition and ability to leverage canonical tricks for constant-time checks in real code paths.

## Key Concepts

- Bit tricks: (x & (x >> 1)) detects adjacent 1s
- Complexity: O(1), no loops
- Edge cases: 0, power-of-two inputs

## Code Example

```javascript
function hasAdjacentOnes(n) {
  return (n & (n >> 1)) !== 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend this to detect at least k consecutive 1s?
- How would you adapt for signed 32-bit integers and two's complement behavior?
